newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian central bank cuts key interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Colombian central bank cuts key interest rates.

text.p: The Colombian central bank's policy-making board of directors cut key interest rates by one percentage point on Tuesday in a bid to breathe new life into the economy, bank officials said.
Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo, who had insisted on a cut of at least 2.0 percent, heralded the decision as "on the mark."
But he also insisted that it was "insufficient" to refuel economic growth, which totaled just 2.08 percent last year against average economic growth of more than 4.0 percent between 1992 and 1995.

Rates on benchmark overnight Treasury bills were cut to 20.50 percent from 21.50 percent, while rates on 30-day and 90- day notes slipped to 22 and 23 percent from 23 and 24 percent respectively, bank officials said.

Central bank director Miguel Urrutia said the drop would be reflected almost immediately in commercial debt rates, but he stressed that any further cut was contingent on the government's ability to meet this year's 18 percent inflation target.
Inflation last year totalled 21.63 percent and annualised inflation in April was running at 18.52 percent.

In his remarks to reporters, Urrutia said the central bank had now cut interest rates by 9.0 percent over the last nine months, a move that has helped boost equities while taking some of the lustre off investment in fixed income securities.

Urrutia said there were "many causes" behind the country's economic slowdown, however, and conceded that slightly lower rates were unlikely to produce a major turnaround. Armando Montenegro, head of the powerful National Financial Industries Association, said that even a 2.0 percent cut in central bank rates was unlikely to offer much hope for a return to solid economic growth anytime soon.

Montenegro and other top analysts have warned repeatedly that fundamental factors, including nagging political uncertainty and a sharp slowdown in the construction sector, are likely to put the government's ambitious 4.0 percent growth target out of reach this year.
